new_statements.rule_in_words: Zou is a tone language (three contrastive lexical tones: level, low-rising, falling, on monosyllabic roots) and the reference grammar states explicitly that word stress and rhythm are not found in the language, so no word-stress placement rule is given. The companion article (Singh & Lukram 2013) and the independent JNU grammar (Tungdim 2012, four Praat-measured tones with the syllable as TBU) describe word prosody purely in terms of tone and never mention stress in Zou.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The only hedge is the table note that '–' means 'absent or need further investigations'. Tungdim 2012 (pp. 286-288) describes tone changes and first-syllable reduction in compounds, but frames them as tone rules, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical phonology of monosyllabic roots and compounds); citation forms. Tungdim 2012 p. 251 names the syllable as the tone-bearing unit. Intonation is listed as present but not analysed for stress interaction.
new_statements.identity_note: yosa1234 is not a distinct language. ISO 639-3 change request 2012-035 (downloaded, 5 pp.) states: "Yos is the English plural form of the name 'Yo', which is just another pronunciation of 'Zo'. Yos/Yo is not a separate group or a separate language. It is the same as 'Zo'. No references to the 'Yos' exist apart from an obscure alleged reference in the 1983 Census of Myanmar." Glottolog's yosa1234 record carries the same iso_retirement block (change_to: zom). The language it denotes is Zou [zom] = zouu1235, which is ALREADY in the catalog (site_bib/lang/: in_catalog true, classification tonal, deciding source Singh & Lukram 2013). by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) yosa1234 should be resolved as an alias of zouu1235, not added as a second entry. The sources quoted below describe Zou of Churachandpur district, Manipur (Lukram 2013) and Zo of Manipur/Myanmar (Tungdim 2012).

Also lists three unread Glottolog items (Tungdim 2011 self-tutor; Zomi 2010 Zolai Gelhmaan; Thang 2001 Proto-Chin reconstruction).

Nothing on stress or tone; lists 23 consonants and 7 vowels and cites Singh & Himmat 2013 'Zou Phonology' (Language in India 13(2): 683-701), Tungdim 2012 'A Descriptive Grammar of the Zo Language', Tungdim 2011 Zo-English-Hindi self-tutor, Haokip 2011.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Silent on stress ('stress'/'accent' absent from the text). Suprasegments section (journal p. 698, PDF p. 16): 'Zou language has three contrastive tones. They are: 1. Level, 2. Low-rising, and 3. Falling.' with 12 minimal triplets (hai 'mango' / ha´i 'chew' / ha`i 'cup, forget'; sa 'hot' / sa´ 'meat' / sa` 'dense, thick'..). Conclusion p. 699: 'It is a tonal language having three degree of tones: level, low-rising, and falling.' This is the catalog's current deciding source for zouu1235.
